newsitem.title: UK: CBI questions value for money of British education.
newsitem.headline: CBI questions value for money of British education.

text.p: The Confederation of British Industry (CBI) on Thursday called for a constructive debate on whether Britain gets value for money from the 36 billion pounds it spends on education every year.

"Achieving the UK's education and training targets must be a national priority, but should we be investing more in education to hit those targets?" CBI director-general Adair Turner asked at the launch of a CBI consultation document on education.
The document suggested ways of working out whether Britain could meet its educational targets without additional spending by using resources more efficiently, the CBI said.

"We don't have enough information yet to have clear answers," Turner said. "The CBI will encourage the government and other key players over the coming months to develop its methodology and fill the current information gaps.

Education is one of the main election battlegrounds in Britain. On Wednesday the Conservative Party announced an expansion of the assisted places scheme which helps children from poorer families attend independent schools.

The opposition Labour Party, hot favourites to take power after elections which must be held by May, has said it will scrap the scheme to pay for its pledge to reduce primary school sizes to no more than 30.
The CBI said it aimed to stimulate debate on the issue of value for money in education and would reach its own conclusions in the autumn.
The CBI said one of the main focuses of its consultation document was whether a redistribution of resources into primary schools would improve attainment. -- London Newsroom +44 171 542 7717
